title: 道德經 第十八章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 18, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 61. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 18 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 俗薄 (Custom Grown Thin). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to be thrown aside, to fall into disuse
there is, there comes to be
humaneness and rightness — the Confucian virtues, named as a pair

sentences.l:
The great Way thrown aside —
there is humaneness and rightness;
sentences.i: When the great Way is thrown aside, humaneness and rightness appear;
sentences.n: Four flat conditionals make up this chapter, and not one of them is marked as a conditional: two clauses are set down side by side and the 'when… then' is the reader's to supply, as with 妄作凶 in chapter 16. 仁 and 義 are the Confucian virtues by their own names, and the chapter is a polemic: a virtue only needs a name once the thing itself has gone. Note that the Guodian bamboo slips (c. 300 BC), the oldest witness we have, read 安有仁義 here. 安 can be the plain 'then there is', but it is also the interrogative 'how would there be?' — which would turn the line inside out. Genuinely undecided.

morph.gloss: artifice, the counterfeit, what is got up by contrivance

sentences.l:
Cleverness comes forth —
there is great counterfeit;
sentences.i: When cleverness appears, great pretence comes with it;
sentences.n: 偽 carries the argument in its own shape: it is 人 'a man' beside 為 'to do' — what is done by human contrivance, and therefore not so of itself. Set it against 自然 at the end of chapter 17 and the two characters are opposites by construction.

sentences.t:
六親不和，
有孝慈；
國家昏亂，
有忠臣。

morph.gloss: the six kinships — the bonds of blood a household is made of
filial devotion, a child's care for a parent
the love that goes down — a parent's tenderness for a child
state and household — the realm (國) and the great families in it (家)
a minister, a servant of the state

sentences.l:
The six kinships out of concord —
there is filial devotion and parental love;
state and household benighted and in disorder —
there are loyal ministers.
sentences.i: When the six bonds of kin fall out of concord, filial devotion and parental love appear; when state and household go dark and fall into disorder, loyal ministers appear.
sentences.n: 六親 names a set: the six relations of blood a household is built from — the usual list is father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, child, though the lists differ. 孝 and 慈 are the two directions of family feeling, up from child to parent and down from parent to child; Chinese has separate words and English does not. Manuscript note: the Mawangdui text reads 邦家 where ours reads 國家. 邦 was the personal name of Liu Bang, who founded the Han, and after his death the character was replaced by 國 throughout the empire's books — the same kind of taboo substitution that put 常 in place of 恆 in chapter 1. Mawangdui also reads 貞臣 'upright ministers' for 忠臣.
